questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Silk Routes Linking the World' refers to.
questions.a: Pre-modern trade and cultural exchange flowed along silk routes, a web of land and sea paths that carried west-bound Chinese silk cargoes alongside pottery, textiles, spices, metals and religious ideas between Asia, Europe and North Africa.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Silk Routes Linking the World'.
questions.a: Christian missionaries and Muslim preachers travelled these routes centuries ago, proving that goods and beliefs moved together across continents.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Silk Routes Linking the World' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Silk Routes Link the World (source: jess303.txt lines 43-60)

concepts.title: Food Travels and the Columbian Exchange

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Food Travels and the Columbian Exchange' refers to.
questions.a: Everyday foods crossed continents long ago, and after Christopher Columbus's voyages the Americas gave potatoes, maize, chillies, tomatoes and sweet potatoes to the world, transforming diets everywhere.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Food Travels and the Columbian Exchange'.
questions.a: Noodles and spaghetti are argued to have travelled from China and Arabia to Italy, showing that trade routes moved recipes as surely as merchandise.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Food Travels and the Columbian Exchange' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Food Travels: Spaghetti and Potato (source: jess303.txt lines 59-97)

concepts.title: Conquest, Disease and Trade after Columbus

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Conquest, Disease and Trade after Columbus' refers to.
questions.a: European conquest of the Americas succeeded less by guns than by germs, since smallpox carried across the Atlantic killed entire communities and cleared the way for colonisation and the global silver trade.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Conquest, Disease and Trade after Columbus'.
questions.a: Until the nineteenth century, poverty and hunger were common in Europe, and the search for food and precious metals drove long-distance commerce.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Conquest, Disease and Trade after Columbus' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Conquest, Disease and Trade (source: jess303.txt lines 98-213)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Nineteenth Century World Economy' refers to.
questions.a: Between 1815 and 1914 a world economy took shape as technology, capital and migration moved together: railways and canals linked farmlands to ports, and roughly 150 million people emigrated from Europe to work in the Americas and Australia.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Nineteenth Century World Economy'.
questions.a: Canal Colonies irrigated by new canals in Punjab turned wasteland into wheat export zones, while corn law abolition in Britain opened food markets to the world.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Nineteenth Century World Economy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Nineteenth Century (1815-1914) (source: jess303.txt lines 214-290)

concepts.title: Rinderpest and the Conquest of Africa

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Rinderpest and the Conquest of Africa' refers to.
questions.a: Rinderpest, a devastating cattle disease, arrived in Africa in the late 1880s and wiped out two-thirds of the cattle, destroying African livelihoods and easing European seizure of land and labour for plantations and mines.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Rinderpest and the Conquest of Africa'.
questions.a: The loss of cattle forced Africans to work for wages, so a virus deepened colonial control of the continent.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Rinderpest and the Conquest of Africa' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Rinderpest, or the Cattle Plague (source: jess303.txt lines 452-510)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Indentured Labour Migration from India' refers to.
questions.a: In the nineteenth century hundreds of thousands of Indian labourers signed contracts of indenture to work on plantations, in mines and in construction across the Caribbean, Mauritius, Fiji, Malaya and Ceylon, under a bonded system of harsh conditions.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Indentured Labour Migration from India'.
questions.a: Recruits came largely from the districts of eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and central India, and songs and memoirs of the workers kept alive the memory of hardship in the sugar and tea colonies.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Indentured Labour Migration from India' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Indentured Labour Migration from India (source: jess303.txt lines 511-628)

concepts.title: British Manufactures and the Indian Economy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'British Manufactures and the Indian Economy' refers to.
questions.a: From the early nineteenth century British machine-made manufactures flooded Indian markets, while India became an exporter of raw materials and foodstuffs and a huge consumer of British goods, tightening its colonial role in the world economy.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'British Manufactures and the Indian Economy'.
questions.a: Indian handicrafts collapsed under imported cloth, and in the reverse direction Britain used India's export surplus to balance its own trade deficits.

questions.q: Under which section is 'British Manufactures and the Indian Economy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Inter-war Economy (source: jess303.txt lines 629-826)

concepts.title: The Great Depression and Its Indian Impact

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Great Depression and Its Indian Impact' refers to.
questions.a: The Great Depression that began around 1929 brought catastrophic declines in production, employment and incomes worldwide, and in India wheat prices fell by 50 per cent between 1928 and 1934 while jute prices collapsed by 60 per cent, driving peasants deeper into debt.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Great Depression and Its Indian Impact'.
questions.a: Agricultural prices fell more sharply than industrial prices, so colonial farmers lost income while urban dwellers with fixed incomes actually gained from cheap goods.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Great Depression and Its Indian Impact' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Great Depression (source: jess303.txt lines 884-1050)

concepts.title: Wheat Price Fall in Per Cent

questions.q: Calculate the fall in wheat price given the percentage decline. Use the method 'Wheat Price Fall in Per Cent'. Work with: fall_percent = 15, old_price = 80000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of price_drop.
questions.a: 12000 units

questions.q: How many rupees did a farmer lose when prices fell 50 per cent? Use the method 'Wheat Price Fall in Per Cent'. Work with: fall_percent = 18, old_price = 20000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of price_drop.
questions.a: 3600 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Wheat Price Fall in Per Cent' refers to.
questions.a: A price fall expressed in per cent converts to an actual drop by multiplying the earlier price by the fall percentage, as with Indian wheat whose price halved during the depression years.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Wheat Price Fall in Per Cent'.
questions.a: Between 1928 and 1934 Indian wheat prices fell 50 per cent and jute prices 60 per cent, so a grower selling at a quarter of the earlier price is consistent with such collapses.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Wheat Price Fall in Per Cent', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: price_drop = old_price * fall_percent / 100

concepts.title: Bretton Woods Institutions and Fixed Exchange Rates

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Bretton Woods Institutions and Fixed Exchange Rates' refers to.
questions.a: The 1944 Bretton Woods conference created the International Monetary Fund to handle member deficits and the World Bank to finance post-war reconstruction, and pegged national currencies to a dollar that was anchored to gold at 35 dollars per ounce.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Bretton Woods Institutions and Fixed Exchange Rates'.
questions.a: The Bretton Woods twins began operations in 1947 under Western industrial control with a US veto, and world trade grew over 8 per cent a year between 1950 and 1970.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Bretton Woods Institutions and Fixed Exchange Rates' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Reconstruction and Bretton Woods Institutions (source: jess303.txt lines 1050-1120)

concepts.title: Gold Value at the Fixed Dollar Price

questions.q: Calculate the dollar value of a given quantity of gold at the bretton woods price. Use the method 'Gold Value at the Fixed Dollar Price'. Work with: gold_ounces = 60. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gold_value.
questions.a: 2100 units

questions.q: How many dollars did one ounce of gold cost under bretton woods? Use the method 'Gold Value at the Fixed Dollar Price'. Work with: gold_ounces = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gold_value.
questions.a: 10500 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Gold Value at the Fixed Dollar Price' refers to.
questions.a: Under the Bretton Woods anchor, gold was valued at a fixed 35 dollars per ounce, so the dollar value of any quantity of gold equals the number of ounces multiplied by 35.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Gold Value at the Fixed Dollar Price'.
questions.a: This fixed price of 35 dollars an ounce held the dollar to gold and kept world currencies stable until the system collapsed in the 1970s.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Gold Value at the Fixed Dollar Price', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: gold_value = gold_ounces * 35

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Decolonisation, G-77 and the NIEO' refers to.
questions.a: After the Second World War most Asian and African colonies became independent but remained poor and resource-strapped, so developing countries organised as the Group of 77 to demand a New International Economic Order with control over resources and fairer prices.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Decolonisation, G-77 and the NIEO'.
questions.a: The Bretton Woods institutions shifted attention to developing countries from the late 1950s, while multinational corporations spread worldwide partly to jump over high import tariffs.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Decolonisation, G-77 and the NIEO' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Decolonisation and Independence (source: jess303.txt lines 1120-1260)
